newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy faces economic ruin without EMU - Prodi.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy faces economic ruin without EMU - Prodi.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi, trying to push through a tough 1997 budget, said on Tuesday that Italy would face economic ruin if it failed to be among the first countries to join a planned single European currency.

"There can no longer be a situation where some arrive first and others later, but there will be a large number of countries that enter right away," Prodi told Italian reporters at the end of a two-day trip to the Netherlands.
"Not being among these countries means economic ruin for Italy," he said in comments broadcast by Italian television.
Prodi also vowed that Italy's 1997 budget, due to be presented on Friday, would help Italy clinch a place in European Monetary Union.
"There is no doubt that this Friday the Italian government will present a budget that will take Italy into Europe," he said.
Prodi told state radio in an interview broadcast on Tuesday he was convinced that political stumbling blocks over the budget would not lead to a crisis in his government.
"There is no risk of a crisis because when there are common objectives the ways and means of arriving at an agreement can be found," he said.
Parties supporting the government failed to reach agreement on Monday after the hard left spurned Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi's call for a tougher package.
The budget has run into serious flak from the hard-left Communist Refoundation party.

Although the party formally is not a part of the coalition, the centre-left government relies on its votes for a majority in the lower house, where the budget has to be ratified by the end of the year.
But Prodi denied that the talks had broken down.
"This (meeting) was neither the conclusion nor the failure of the negotiations. We made some good progress. We still have to go forward because the problem is very complex," he said.

Ciampi has already announced that the package will cut 32.4 trillion lire ($21.2 billion) off next year's deficit, but several Italian newspapers reported on Tuesday that the budget might have to cut as much as 40.0 trillion lire.
Ciampi, worried that Italy is falling behind in its bid to join the first wave of countries, has demanded that the budget should tackle some sensitive areas of welfare spending.
His call was backed by Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio, who hinted at the weekend that a tough budget might be rewarded with an interest rate cut.

EMU founder members have to cut the ratio between their annual budget deficit and gross domestic product to no more than three percent by the end of 1997. Italy is forecasting a deficit/GDP ratio of 6.09 percent this year and 4.52 percent next.
